prompt.context: Our client is Grocery Save grocery chain. They have about 200 grocery stores. They are a full-range store including groceries, pet food, clothing etc. Some stores include banks, dry cleaners, and post offices. A few others include child care, flower shops and catering. They were doing very well for the last several years but from the last 2 years their market share growth is down. Their margins have been falling. Their average sales per store has been decreasing. Walmart has opened 4 super centers which contain 75% of the same collection of items. They plan to open even more stores.
prompt.question: How do we reverse the decline in store sales? How do we successfully compete with Walmart?

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of stores have the additional services like banks, dry cleaners, post offices, child care, flower shops, and catering?
clarifying_info.a: 15% have banks, dry cleaners and post offices; whereas 5% have child care, flower shops, and catering. The remaining are regular stores.

clarifying_info.q: Does each shop have the ability to change prices or is it centrally governed for all 200 stores?
clarifying_info.a: Each store has the ability to set their own prices.

exhibits.title: Market Research: Customer Perception by Attribute
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing Walmart, Stop & Shop, and Grocery Save across six customer perception attributes: Store prices, Good deals, Organic meat, Healthy foods, Convenience of locations, and Shopping experience. Each bar shows the percentage of positive responses per retailer per attribute.
exhibits.data: Attributes compared: Store prices, Good deals, Organic meat, Healthy foods, Convenience of locations, Shopping experience; Retailers compared: Walmart, Stop & Shop, Grocery Save; Scale: 0% to 100%

framework: Understand root causes of declining average sales per store (segmentation, location, competition, pricing, marketing, customer service, store format mix)
Assess competitive positioning vs. Walmart and nearest competitors on price and non-price dimensions
Identify actions to change customer price perception and improve shopping experience
Quantify the cost/impact of price reduction initiatives
Develop a strategic recommendation leveraging Grocery Save's competitive advantages

questions.prompt: What are the reasons for the decline of average sales per store?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers multiple buckets: targeting the wrong customer segment; incorrect or unfavorable store locations with many nearby competitors; inadequate marketing; pricing too high relative to competitors; poor customer service; lack of convenience; owned vs. franchise incentive misalignment (franchise contracts may not motivate pushing sales); broader economic headwinds; only 5% of stores are full-service one-stop shops whereas competitors may offer more; some stores may be unprofitable and dragging the average down.

questions.prompt: Consumers perceive Grocery Save prices to be 20% greater than Walmart, and also higher than the nearest competitor even though actual prices are similar. What actions can the marketing manager take to change the customer's perception of prices?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: direct-to-consumer marketing campaigns highlighting value; targeted discounts and promotions; selectively lowering prices of items known to be significantly higher than competitors; expanding value-added services to justify perceived premium; loyalty/rewards program to reward repeat customers; auditing and adjusting prices of affiliated services (dry cleaning, etc.) since high ancillary prices may create an overall expensive image; reviewing franchise vs. owned-store incentives to ensure price competitiveness at the store level.

questions.prompt: The store decides to bring down the prices of the fastest-selling 6,000 items by 15%. How much would it cost the company? Use the data provided.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the revenue base for the fastest 6,000 items, apply the 15% price reduction to compute lost revenue per store, then scale across all 200 stores. Rounding 9.6M to 10M is acceptable and shows numerical comfort.

math.setup: Average sales per store = $40M. Fastest 6,000 items account for 24% of store sales. Price reduction = 15%. Number of stores = 200.
steps: Sales of fastest 6,000 items per store = 40M x 24% = 9.6M (round to ~10M)
Impact on profit per store = 15% x 10M = 1.5M
Total impact across all 200 stores = 200 x 1.5M = 300M
math.answer: The price reduction would cost the company approximately $300M per year.

questions.prompt: Analyze the market research exhibit showing customer perceptions across Store prices, Good deals, Organic meat, Healthy foods, Convenience of locations, and Shopping experience for Walmart, Stop & Shop, and Grocery Save. What are the strategic implications?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: Grocery Save performs well on Convenience of locations, Healthy foods, and Organic meat — these are competitive advantages to market more aggressively. Grocery Save underperforms on Store prices and Shopping experience — these are priority areas for improvement. The price perception gap reinforces the need for marketing and operational action on pricing. Shopping experience is an area where Grocery Save can differentiate from Walmart on a non-price basis.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions should Grocery Save take to reverse the decline in average sales per store and successfully compete with Walmart?

categories.name: Pricing & Perception
ideas: Reduce prices on fastest-selling items to close the perceived 20% gap with Walmart
Launch a price-matching or price-transparency campaign
Audit affiliated service prices (dry cleaning, etc.) that may create an expensive brand image
Introduce a loyalty program with visible discounts for repeat customers

categories.name: Marketing & Positioning
ideas: Aggressively market competitive advantages: convenience of locations, healthy foods, organic meat
Direct-to-consumer campaigns highlighting value and quality
Targeted promotions and coupons for key customer segments
Reposition brand around health, freshness, and community rather than competing on price alone

categories.name: Shopping Experience
ideas: Redesign store layout to improve navigation and comfort
Improve customer service training and staffing
Reduce checkout wait times
Enhance in-store ambiance and cleanliness

categories.name: Store Format & Services
ideas: Expand full-service one-stop-shop model (child care, flower shop, catering) beyond current 5% of stores
Assess whether 15% partial-service stores should add more services
Close or reformat underperforming stores dragging down the average
Pilot new service offerings in high-traffic locations

categories.name: Competitive Response to Walmart
ideas: Focus on segments Walmart cannot serve well: premium/organic, local community, personalized service
Leverage convenience of more locations vs. Walmart's fewer super centers
Explore partnerships with local suppliers for differentiated product assortment
Avoid direct price war on commodity items; compete on value-added dimensions

recommendation: Improve the overall shopping experience to differentiate Grocery Save from Walmart on a non-price dimension

Aggressively market and invest in Grocery Save's proven competitive advantages — convenience of locations, healthy foods, and organic meat — to attract and retain value-conscious and health-oriented shoppers

Reduce prices on high-visibility fastest-selling items and improve marketing around pricing to close the customer perception gap, accepting an estimated $300M annual cost impact that must be offset by volume gains and cost efficiencies
risks: A $300M price reduction is a significant profit hit; volume uplift must materialize quickly or margins worsen further
Walmart can out-invest Grocery Save on price indefinitely — a pure price war is not sustainable
Expanding one-stop-shop services requires capital and operational expertise in non-core areas
next_steps: Conduct store-level profitability analysis to identify and address underperforming stores
Pilot the price reduction on fastest-selling items in a subset of stores and measure volume response before full rollout
Develop a phased plan to upgrade shopping experience across all 200 stores
Launch a targeted marketing campaign emphasizing convenience, health, and organic credentials within 90 days
